https://www.euronews.com/2026/08/09/part.text: In Budapest, the emergence of the so-called Ínség-szikla (Famine Rock) by the Liberty Bridge signals that there is too little water in the Danube. The stretch of riverbed beneath the central pillar of Margaret Bridge is surfacing more and more often each year, and an ever-larger area is left dry.Photographer Zsanett Zsebők shared a video on Facebook of a Saturday night pop-up party, unleashing a flood of comments. Those with a more relaxed outlook say a spontaneous party like this is very cool, even if it takes place on the dried-out central section of the Danube Riverbed. Others see it instead as a horrifying natural disaster that is increasingly reshaping summers in Europe, especially in Hungary.In 2018, the underwater extension of the Margit Island shoal on the other side of the Margit Bridge, towards the Parliament, became accessible even in shoes. Since then, this has been happening more frequently, for longer periods, and over a larger area.László Wild, the heritage architect who led the most recent reconstruction of Margaret Bridge, said in an earlier interview that the Danube Riverbed along the Budapest section is in an incredible state of disorder.In previous years, the same metal rubbish bins that were common in Budapest before the Second World War have always turned up here; even the remains of the pillars from the scaffolding that was presumably used by Ernest Goüin’s team until 1876, during the years of the bridge’s construction.As the dried-out area expands, more and more people are walking across from Margaret Island. From there, the city’s panorama can be seen from a new angle, looking particularly beautiful in the evening lights. At first, concern about global warming merely left passers-by somewhat taken aback, but now the party crowd has appeared as well.Legend has it that not only did the band keep playing on the sinking Titanic until the very last moment, but some guests even joked that they wanted to get ice for their cocktails from the iceberg itself. The receding Danube evokes the same duality: in some people it sparks worry and anxiety, in others it brings out the urge to live in the carpe diem spirit.

https://www.budapesttimes.hu/travel/a-ta.text: The Budapest Times A Tale of Two Tallinns – part 2 Written by Alexander Stemp Today, after just returning from a few days in the Estonian capital Tallinn, I can now offer the finale to my “Tale of Two Tallinns” story, part one of which took place five years ago when I visited Szolnok, 100 kilometres east of Budapest, and which has now reached completion in the Baltic nation this September 2026. To recap, it was while on that outing to Szolnok in 2021 that the most unexpected and extraordinary thing happened, completely catching me out. A bus displaying an illuminated destination sign “Tallinn” passed by, something that probably won’t mean anything to most people but it did to me, because shortly before I had been on a family holiday in Estonia and seen the real Tallinn. So this Baltic location and memory were still very much alive in my mind. See A tale of two Tallinns for part one. I recall that I wasn’t feeling too well and was concerned for my dizzy state on that particular day in central Szolnok. Then, while sitting on a road-side bench to regain my senses, another “Tallinn” bus drove by. Again I was startled but relieved that this was perhaps no imaginary matter after all. Suddenly curiosity got the better of me as I perked up and became intrigued by this remarkable finding. As then an assignment finally came to me, and possibly an article too. The first thing I did was to approach the nearest bus stop and look at the timetable. All became clear: it was not just “Tallinn” in itself, as assumed, but “Tallinn Városrész”, meaning “Tallinn Town Reserve,” and clearly this was a nearby suburb. But why the Estonian name? When the next Tallinn bus came I hopped on and eventually arrived at the mysterious end stop, finding myself within the confines of the tower block district of the Szolnok suburbs. And that was it. Slowly the Tallinn illusion began to fade, as there was not a trace of Estonian life or culture to be seen. Certainly there wasn’t much to celebrate but at least this gave me something to work on. However, I found that there was almost no online research available about this very obscure matter, but fortunately an old friend told me that during the former regime Szolnok was Tallinn’s sister city. The two-way link ended, though, and Szolnok is now twinned with another Estonian town, Rakvere in the east of the country. Fortunately I discovered one tiny redeeming feature in the Szolnok, Hungary, archive files: there was once the Tallinn Club Cinema, built in 1973. This retro relic was on 9 Kálmán Kandó Square but closed years ago. I walked around with my mobile phone and hoped to find a trace, but alas my efforts came to no avail. However, eventually I discovered online that in the outskirts of Tallinn, Estonia, there is a small hub called “Szolnok”. Although this must come as a tribute to Hungary’s Szolnok, judging by what I saw on Google Maps and in photographs, there is not much difference between Szolnok in Tallinn and Tallinn in Szolnok, as both districts are clearly residential only. But I determined that when I returned to the Baltic Tallinn I would visit its Szolnok to complete this impulsive matter. The Tale of Two Szolnoks And so, I made my eventual return to the Estonian capital this September 2026 and made my way to the main Balti Jamm, the central train station. From there it was the number 85 bus and 20 minutes later I was in Baltic Szolnok, which features on the busy, main “Eduard Vilde tee” road. Szolnok in Tallinn, Estonia When I arrived it became apparent that apart from the obvious bus stop signs on both sides of this road, unfortunately there was no hidden treasure to be found. But at least Szolnok in Estonia existed, albeit with nothing Hungarian related while I was there. It was a rainy evening and after walking around that immediate area for about 20 minutes all I saw was an abundance of tower blocks, a few simple shops and the busy main road. With my mobile phone I took my tokenish souvenirs of the Szolnok bus stop signs and returned to the hotel. This outcome was not too surprising. At least I have the small satisfaction of knowing the mission is accomplished. Certainly the similarities between these two suburbs match and complement one another. Hopefully this matter may compliment me as I enjoy these kinds of irregular excursions. Finally – and beyond obsessing over bus stops, tower blocks and remote nondescript suburbs – Tallinn and Szolnok are great places and very much worth visiting.
